# The Last Crossing

On the last morning of the ferry, someone left a refrigerator on the east landing. It stood with its door open and a paper sign taped to the butter compartment: STILL GOOD.

Ruth went down with her coffee to investigate. The refrigerator smelled faintly of oranges. Inside it, on the middle shelf, was a single blue ice tray, empty except for a dead wasp.

The sign seemed an ambitious claim, but she supposed the person who had written it knew more about the refrigerator than she did.

At six, she unchained the gate and started the engine. The river was low enough that a shopping cart had emerged near the pilings. By afternoon, if the level kept dropping, she would be able to see what was in it. There was usually something in it. The river was not a person, whatever the poets at the library liked to say, but it did have a habit of putting things inside other things.

The first passenger was Mr. Teague, who had taken the 6:10 to the west bank every weekday for thirty-two years. He used to work at the bakery. Now he crossed to read the newspaper in a café where they got a different newspaper from the one he got at home.

“Fridge yours?” Ruth asked.

“No,” he said, in a tone that suggested she had made a personal remark.

He handed her a nickel. The ferry had been free since 1998, but that was the year his wife died, and he had aged into certain habits without bothering to distinguish which ones belonged to grief. Ruth put the nickel in the jar with the others.

“See you at four,” he said on the far bank.

“Three forty-five is the last return.”

“I know what the sign says.”

She waited.

“I’ll see you at three forty-five,” he said.

The bridge had opened on Monday. It was a clean, pale structure a mile downstream, with a lane for bicycles and a series of decorative openings through which, if you were unfortunate enough to drop your phone, you could watch it fall for quite a long time. Ruth had walked across with everybody else. From the middle, she could see the ferry’s entire route. Seen that way, it was a discouragingly small piece of water.

At the opening ceremony, a county commissioner had said that the bridge would bring both halves of the town together. Ruth wondered what he thought she had been doing all these years, but she was willing to concede that he meant at night, in winter, with an ambulance. She had once carried a woman in labor during a thunderstorm. It had taken eleven minutes, and for all eleven the woman had squeezed Ruth’s wrist so hard that Ruth felt it the following day. If anybody had suggested a bridge at the time, she would have voted for it on the spot.

Still, it was one thing to want the bridge and another to be told how happy she must be about it.

At seven fifteen, her brother came down the ramp carrying two cartons of eggs. He set them on the bench and stepped back onto the landing.

“Get on or get off,” Ruth said.

“I’m off.”

“You’ve left eggs.”

“They’re for you.”

“I don’t need twenty-four eggs.”

“Neither do I. That’s how you got them.”

Cal had been raising chickens for six months. He had a particular talent for beginning hobbies that became other people’s work. At Christmas he had given Ruth a sourdough starter with a name and a feeding schedule. She had put it in the refrigerator and forgotten about it until May, by which time it looked capable of feeding itself.

“You coming this afternoon?” she asked.

“For what?”

She looked at him.

“Oh,” he said. “I didn’t know you wanted me to.”

Ruth had wanted him to figure out that she wanted him to. Until he said it, she hadn’t realized how much work that required of him, or how little it required of her.

“Three forty-five,” she said.

“Okay.” He stood there another moment. “You need a ride home after?”

“I have my car.”

“I know. It was an offer, not a theory.”

He went up the ramp. Halfway to the road, he stopped at the refrigerator and tested the seal with his thumb.

At nine, a woman and a boy came aboard with a folding chair. The woman set up the chair although there were two perfectly good benches. The boy pressed his face between the railings. He wanted to know how deep the river was, and Ruth told him it depended where you asked.

“Here,” he said.

“About twelve feet.”

He considered it. “If you stood on my mom’s head, and I stood on yours?”

“I’d want to talk to your mom about it first.”

The woman laughed. She said they used to ride the ferry when he was a baby, because it was the only place he would sleep. She had spent whole afternoons going back and forth. Did Ruth remember?

Ruth had a faint recollection of a red blanket. What she remembered more clearly was a young woman who got on in the rain one day without a coat. Ruth had offered her the old sweater she kept in the wheelhouse. The woman said no, then yes, then cried while trying to get her hand through the sleeve. Ruth had steered one-handed so she could hold the cuff open. She didn’t know if it was this woman. There had been a lot of rain and a lot of people.

“Was there a red blanket?” she asked.

“Yellow,” the woman said. “I still have it. I put it under the washing machine when it shakes.”

At the west landing the boy announced that he wanted to cross again immediately. His mother folded her chair and said they would walk back over the bridge. It seemed to Ruth that the boy would protest, but he wanted to see how the decorative holes worked.

By eleven the sun had burned through the cloud cover. Ruth opened the wheelhouse windows and found, under the logbook, a letter she had been carrying for four months. It was from the county and informed her of the disposition of the ferry. She liked that word. It made the boat sound bad-tempered.

The parks department was going to take it upriver and use it to carry maintenance crews out to the islands. The benches would come off, and someone would paint over the blue stripes. Ruth had been invited to train the new operator, but she’d declined. The boat was easy to drive. The hard part was getting the hang of the approaches, and at the islands there would be different approaches for somebody else to get the hang of.

She folded the letter and put it in her pocket. Then she got it out again and read the second page, which she had never read. The county wanted the keys left in the lockbox and the fuel tank at least a quarter full. Further down was a blank headed OPERATOR REMARKS.

Ruth took out her pen. She had never found a way to stop the rattle in the port window except to wedge a folded coffee sleeve into the frame. The fuel gauge stuck at half for about an hour after you filled the tank. When you shut the wheelhouse door too hard in cold weather, the latch could drop on the inside and lock you out. She had spent that particular February crossing steering with a boat hook through the open window, in full view of a passenger who was polite enough to look at his sandwich the entire time.

She wrote down all three things. There was room for a fourth, but she couldn’t think of one until she started to put the pen away.

*The horn is louder on deck than you think.*

At noon an unfamiliar man came aboard, saluted, and asked if he could scatter his father’s ashes. He had a white paper bag with a bakery logo on it. Ruth said he could if he wanted, but the wind was blowing straight down the deck, and he might not get the result he was picturing.

The man looked at the bag.

“It’s rolls,” he said. “I was going to ask where a person could scatter ashes. My sister has the ashes.”

“Oh,” Ruth said. “Well. That’ll be easier on your rolls.”

He sat on the bench and opened the bag. His father had grown up on the east bank and moved away at seventeen. As far as the man could tell, he had spent the next sixty years threatening to move back. His children were trying to decide how literally to take him.

“Did he ever mention a particular spot?” Ruth asked.

“He always talked about the bakery.”

“You can’t scatter him in the bakery.”

“I figured.”

They ate the rolls, which were shiny on top and just underdone in the middle. Ruth suggested a place upstream where the town had put in a couple of benches. The man asked what you could see from there.

“Mostly the people on the other bench,” she said. “But it’s nice in the evening.”

His sister was driving in from Ohio. He decided he would take her to look at it before they did anything. When they reached the landing, he thanked Ruth for her help. He left the last roll in the bag for her, and later, when she had it with coffee, she found that it was the only one with raisins.

Around two the people with cameras began to arrive. A girl from the local paper asked Ruth how many trips she’d made, and Ruth said she didn’t know. The girl asked if she could make an estimate.

“How exact do you need it to sound?”

The girl lowered her phone. “My editor said not to come back with ‘countless.’”

Together, on the back of the county letter, they worked it out. They subtracted the winters the river froze and the year the gearbox went, then added the Saturdays Ruth had covered for Eddie before he retired. They arrived at forty-one thousand, which Ruth distrusted immediately. It was possible to imagine a thousand crossings. She could account for almost that many by thinking about the times she had carried a particular dog. But forty-one thousand was just a big number on the back of a letter. It gave her no more idea of where the time had gone than the mileage on her car.

“Say around forty thousand,” Ruth told the girl.

“Did you ever get bored?”

“Oh, absolutely.”

The girl looked up, pleased, and Ruth saw that this was going to be the quote.

At three thirty, there was a line down the west ramp. Ruth walked along it counting heads. Two bicycles counted as four people, a rule she had made up long ago and could no longer explain, except by asking anybody who disputed it to stand where the bicycles were.

She counted thirty-one. The limit was thirty.

“You can leave me,” said Mr. Teague from the back. “I know how to walk across a bridge.”

Before Ruth could answer, one of the cyclists rolled his bicycle out of line. He said he had been planning to try the new bike lane anyway. This left room for Mr. Teague and, a minute later, for Cal, who came down the ramp with his shirt sticking to his chest. He’d parked on the east bank and walked over the bridge.

“What for?” Ruth asked.

“So I could come back with you.”

He said it plainly, almost impatiently. She was glad he hadn’t said it in a nicer way, in front of all those people.

Mr. Teague offered her his nickel. She got the jar from the wheelhouse and let him drop it in himself. The jar was an old glass one, with a chip on the rim and a picture of a peach. He lifted it a little to see what it weighed.

“You know,” he said, “I started doing that because I had so damn many nickels.”

“Where’d they come from?”

“My wife used to find them in the laundry. Put them in a bowl for me to take upstairs.” He set the jar back down. “I never took them upstairs.”

Ruth blew the horn. Everybody on deck jumped except Cal, who had put his fingers in his ears. When she looked back a moment later, he was helping Mr. Teague settle onto the bench. She untied the line, looped it over the rail, and went inside to take the ferry out.

There was applause as they left the landing. It stopped fairly quickly. A man in a blue cap kept clapping after everyone else had quit, then looked around and quit too. People adjusted their bags and moved out of the sun. Mrs. Avery from the post office told her husband not to take any more pictures of her from below. One of the bicycles tipped over with a sound that made several people think of something they had forgotten to do at home.

Halfway across, Cal came into the wheelhouse.

“Anything I can do?”

“Get me those eggs before somebody sits on them.”

He brought them inside. There was a dark spot on the bottom of one carton where an egg had broken. He held it over the wastebasket and picked out the shell. Ruth watched him wipe each of the neighboring eggs with a paper towel. He turned them gently in his big hands. It was the sort of thing she would have told him not to bother doing if she’d had her hands free to take the carton away from him.

“Where do you want them?” he asked.

“Leave them there. Can you get the line when we come in?”

“I don’t know how.”

“I’ll show you.”

She slowed the engine a touch early so there would be time to tell him where to stand and what to do. When the landing came alongside, he dropped the loop short of the cleat. On his second try he got it over, and Ruth reached down from the wheelhouse to show him how much slack to leave. By then everybody was already waiting at the gate, looking past it toward the road.

On shore, somebody had closed the refrigerator door. Ruth watched the passengers pass it and start up the slope, some turning left toward the parking lot, others heading for the shops. Mr. Teague stayed at the foot of the ramp, studying the printed schedule. She was going to call out to him when he took a pen from his pocket, peeled the schedule out of its plastic sleeve, and turned it over. He wrote something on the back and slid it in again. Then he put on his hat and went home.

Ruth had three things left to do: record the engine hours, check the fuel, and put the keys in the lockbox. She did them in that order. The last one took the longest because she had to find a screwdriver to pry the ferry key off her ring. Her house key was almost the same shape, and for years she had told them apart by touch, by a little notch in the boat key that caught her thumbnail. She worked the screwdriver around until the key came loose. The ring went back in her pocket feeling no lighter at all.

Up on the landing, Cal had opened his truck. He was taking junk out of the bed so there would be room for the refrigerator. So far he’d removed a bent rake, a pail full of smaller pails, and a folding lawn chair Ruth recognized as hers.

“You know if it works?” she asked.

“No.”

“You know where you’re putting it?”

“No.”

She handed him her eggs and took hold of the refrigerator on the side with the hinge. They shifted it a few inches before discovering that neither had a grip. Cal fetched a blanket from the truck, and they tipped the refrigerator onto it and dragged it to the tailgate. The whole operation took ten minutes. Twice they had to stop laughing before they could lift.

When they were done, Ruth went back down to see what Mr. Teague had written. On the back of the schedule, in small square letters, was *THANK YOU RUTH*. Underneath, after what must have been some thought about available space, he’d added *AND EDDIE*.

She left it in the sleeve. Coming back up the ramp, she looked down between the pilings. The water had dropped another inch or two, and she could see a pale oval in the shopping cart. For weeks she’d been hoping it was a porcelain sink. It was a hubcap. She stood there long enough to make sure.

Cal called from the truck to ask about supper. He was going to fry some eggs, he said, if she knew anybody who wanted eggs.

Ruth looked toward her car. Tomorrow she could walk over and get it. She’d have to go the long way, which meant she could stop in the middle of the bridge, if there weren’t too many bicycles, and see what the new operator made of the landing.

“Let’s go,” she said, and got in on the passenger side.
